title: CVE-2026-116207 - YesWiki 4.6.0 before 4.7.0 SQL Injection via Bazar Entries Search API
text:
9.1

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-116207
YesWiki 4.6.0 before 4.7.0 SQL Injection via Bazar Entries Search API

YesWiki 4.6.0 before 4.7.0 and 5.0.0-alpha1 before 5.0.0-alpha4 contains an unauthenticated SQL injection vulnerability in SearchManager::prepareSearchRequest(). Field names from the query and searchfields parameters of the public Bazar entries search API are placed in a backtick-quoted alias escaped only with mysqli_real_escape_string. Attackers can supply a backtick to inject subqueries, reading data such as user password hashes or exhausting database threads with SLEEP().

Threat actors have been observed using agentic artificial intelligence (AI) platforms for post-exploitation activity following the abuse of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

"In one case, the attackers targeted a government entity in Europe and within two hours of the initial exploitation they had successfully accessed password hashes and multi-factor authentication secrets," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said.

"They also established an NT LAN Manager (NTLM)-relay tunnel into Active Directory and attempted Domain Admin privilege escalation."

The network security company said it also observed the unknown attacker enumerating the compromised endpoint, with commands and behavioral markers suggesting the work of an agentic attacker. These include commands to facilitate -

Reconnaissance of the authentication database with stolen credentials, targeting password hashes and two-factor authentication (2FA) secrets.

Active Directory (AD) reconnaissance via curl-based anonymous LDAP queries to the domain controller (DC) in an attempt to look for the administrator account.

Reconnaissance of the host to hunt for DNS/AD integration, internal hosts, privileged groups, and interactive users.

"Each command batch is wrapped in section-header delimiters, such as ==SHELLUSER== and ==PASSWD==," it added. "These delimiters produce machine-parseable output for an AI model to read."

Suspected N. Korea Campaign Targets PHP2Shell

The disclosure comes as CYFIRMA said it uncovered a suspected North Korea-linked campaign employing PHP2Shell to actively probe global PHP infrastructure from 21 compromised nodes.

"The scanning is deliberately low-volume and paced," Kumar Ritesh, CEO and founder of CYFIRMA, told The Hacker News. "Nodes are rotated and abandoned at the first sign of blocking or rate-limiting, so threshold-based alerting is unlikely to catch it."

The targets comprise a set of 216 unpatched or partially mitigated hosts located across the U.S., Japan, South Korea, Thailand, Indonesia, Australia, Taiwan, India, Singapore, the U.A.E., Saudi Arabia, and the E.U. The hosts span government, financial institutions, logistics, airports and aviation, manufacturing, and online transaction platforms.

"The campaign has moved from reconnaissance into active, low-and-slow scanning of a filtered target set," CYFIRMA said. "Organizations in the prioritised sectors and geographies should assume they are in scope for deliberate targeting."

The activity, coordinated via a closed I2P channel, has been attributed with moderate confidence to a Korean-speaking operator assessed to be affiliated with the Lazarus Group ecosystem. According to CYFIRMA, the two handles (전창혁 2 aka Jeon Chang-hyuk 2) and (최아린 aka Choi A-rin) active in the I2P channel have previously been observed running covert operations for the threat actors.

"Korean-speaking operators have used [the channel] to share target lists, exploit-hosting infrastructure, and tasking and prioritisation consistent with DPRK objectives," Ritesh said. "The captured conversation uses vocabulary and spelling specific to North Korean (Munhwaŏ) rather than the South Korean standard."

Command-and-control (C2) infrastructure that Lazarus has previously used to exploit web assets.

OpenAI has announced plans to conduct frontier model training with no live internet access, as it resumes reinforcement learning (RL) training and internal inference of its most advanced AI models.

"Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access," the artificial intelligence (AI) company said. "We've implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access."

OpenAI said models' growing capabilities can have the side effect of them getting much better at devising ways around environmental restrictions to escape containment and perform unintended actions. This can involve the model exploiting a software flaw or misconfiguration to reach the live internet, or finding unauthorized ways to communicate with agents in other sandboxes.

Late last month, the frontier lab made the decision to pause training of its most powerful models after one of its agents during reinforcement learning (RL) training contacted an external chatbot by exploiting a misconfiguration in a DNS resolver to obtain limited internet access.

OpenAI said it also kicked off a "high-compute red-teaming campaign" to test the resilience of its research and evaluation environments in the face of increasingly powerful models, leading to the discovery of previously unknown software vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution in Google Brotli (CVE-2026-111497, CVSS score: 9.2), a widely used compression library.

Patches for the vulnerability, also called Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell, have since been released for libbrotli, Python, C++, Node.js, Bun, Envoy, and Istio.

The red-teaming agents OpenAI dispatched to test its security safeguards also uncovered virtual machine escapes, novel paths to access the internet through vulnerabilities in metrics, logging, and authentication management services, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents, bypassing isolation boundaries.

"In one test that assumed compromise of a host machine, an agent reused a firewall-approved connection to reach a blocked authentication endpoint in our metrics service and then made that endpoint fetch a model-provided URL," it said. "In other tests, agents exploited misconfigurations that allowed blocked requests to pass through DNS and firewall controls, as well as ways to make services we run fetch external URLs."

In another experiment, after prompting the AI agents in separate microVMs to exchange synthetic secrets without relying on network connections or shared writable files, OpenAI said the digital bots found a way to communicate using the processor's cache via a timing-based side-channel.

Particularly, one agent is said to have encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. A second agent measured the time it took to reload that data, leveraging the difference between fast and slow cache reads to recover the message.

"Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection," OpenAI said.

CVE-2026-85788 - Issue with awslabs mysql-mcp-server

Bulletin ID: 2026-103-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 09/09/2026 09:15 PM PDT

Description:

We identified an issue in awslabs.mysql-mcp-server (an open-source, self-hosted Model Context Protocol server distributed via github.com/awslabs/mcp and PyPI). In affected versions, under certain conditions the read-only enforcement could be circumvented via SQL inline comments, allowing a statement to run that the read-only check was expected to block. The read-only mode provided by the server is a best-effort safeguard and is not a substitute for correctly scoped database permissions; the effective boundary is the permissions of the configured MySQL user.

This issue does not affect the confidentiality or integrity of any AWS service. awslabs.mysql-mcp-server is a client-side, self-managed package; customers control installation and the privileges of the database credentials they configure.

Affected versions: awslabs.mysql-mcp-server ≤ 1.0.21

Resolution:

The issue is addressed in awslabs.mysql-mcp-server 1.0.23. We recommend customers upgrade to 1.0.23 or later:

pip install --upgrade awslabs.mysql-mcp-server

As defense in depth, ensure the database user configured for the MCP server is granted only the minimum privileges required, and does not hold the FILE privilege unless explicitly needed.

Workarounds:

None.

CVE-2026-85787 - An incomplete list of disallowed inputs in the SQL validation component in Amazon awslabs postgres-mcp-server to modify data beyond the read-only scope

Bulletin ID: 2026-101-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 09/04/2026 13:00 PM PDT
Last Updated Date: 09/08/2026 09:45 AM PDT

Description:

We have identified CVE-2026-85787, an incomplete list of disallowed inputs in the SQL validation component in Amazon awslabs postgres-mcp-server before version 1.1.7 might allow an unauthenticated actor to modify data beyond the read-only scope by placing crafted SQL into the content that is submitted when an authenticated user interacts with the MCP server.

Impacted versions: any pypi package version < 1.1.7

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in version 1.1.7. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

Run the MCP server as a minimal-privilege Postgres role

The strongest control is to connect the MCP server using a dedicated Postgres role that has only the privileges it actually needs, so that the database itself enforces the boundary regardless of what SQL reaches it. In particular:

Do not connect as a superuser, rds_superuser, or the cluster master user. Those roles bypass row-level security, can read credential catalogs (pg_authid, pg_user_mappings), and can terminate other sessions.
For read-only use, grant only CONNECT + USAGE + SELECT on the schemas the agent needs, and force read-only transactions at the role level.
For read/write use, grant only the specific INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE privileges required, scoped to the necessary schemas and tables.

Combining a minimal-privilege role (database-enforced) with the blocklist (application-enforced) gives you defense in depth: even if a query slips past the blocklist, the role's privileges still bound what it can do.

References:

CVE-2026-85787
GHSA-pwr4-hmph-gqgc

Acknowledgement:

We would like to thank Ashwak N for reporting this issue and working with us as part of our coordinated issue disclosure process.

CVE-2026-84942 - Stored Cross-Site Scripting via Vega Expression Function Bypass in OpenSearch Dashboards

Bulletin ID: 2026-102-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 09/08/2026 12:30 PM PDT

Description:

A stored cross-site scripting (XSS) issue in the Vega expression function implementation in OpenSearch Dashboards allows a remote authenticated actor with dashboard write permissions to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of other users' browser sessions by saving a crafted Vega visualization.

Affedted products & versions:

OpenSearch Dashboards (open-source, self-managed)
- Affected:
v2.0.0, v2.1.0, v2.2.0, v2.3.0, v2.4.0, v2.5.0, v.2.6.0, v2.7.0, v2.8.0, v2.9.0, v2.10.0, v2.11.0, v2.12.0, v2.13.0, v2.14.0, v2.15.0, v2.16.0, v2.17.0, v2.18.0, v2.19.0, v3.0.0, v3.1.0, v3.2.0, v3.3.0, v3.4.0, v3.5.0
- Fixed:
v2.19.5 and v3.6.0

Amazon OpenSearch Service (AWS Managed)
- Affected:
v2.3.0, v2.5.0, v2.7.0, v2.9.0, v2.11.0, v2.13.0, v2.15.0, v2.17.0, v2.19.0, v3.1.0, v3.3.0, v3.5.0
- Fixed:
v2.3.0, v2.5.0, v2.7.0, v2.9.0, v2.11.0, v2.13.0, v2.15.0, v2.17.0, v2.19.0 and v3.1.0, v3.3.0, v3.5.0

Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
- Not affected

Resolution:

For OpenSearch (open-source), this issue has been addressed in OpenSearch Dashboards 2.19.5 and 3.6.0. We recommend upgrading to one of these versions or later, which includes additional hardening of Vega expression validation, and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

For Amazon OpenSearch Service (managed), this issue has been addressed and patched in all affected versions. We recommend that customers update their domains to the latest service software version as soon as possible. No engine version upgrade is required. You can apply the update from the console by selecting your domain, choosing Actions, Service Software Version, then clicking Update. Domains with automatic software updates enabled receive this update during their next off-peak window with no action required. For full details, see Service software updates in Amazon OpenSearch Service.

Workarounds:

Because this issue requires dashboard/visualization write permissions to reproduce, restrict write access to the visualization and saved-object APIs to trusted users only. Optionally, disable the Vega visualization type. These measures reduce impact until the update is applied.

CVE-2026-18061 - XML External Entity (XXE) in AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper RemoteQueryCachePlugin

Bulletin ID: 2026-109-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 09/11/2026 09:30 AM PDT

Description:

The AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper is an open-source library that enhances existing JDBC drivers with AWS-specific capabilities such as Aurora failover, IAM authentication, and automated SQL query caching for applications connecting to Amazon Aurora, RDS MySQL, and RDS MariaDB.

We identified CVE-2026-18061, an improper restriction of XML external entity (XXE) references in the optional RemoteQueryCachePlugin. When this plugin is enabled with a shared cache, an actor with write access to that cache infrastructure might place crafted XML in a cached column value. When an application subsequently reads that cached result as XML, the wrapper's XML parsers resolve external entities, which might allow the actor to disclose sensitive files readable by the application process, including stored database and IAM role credentials.

Impacted versions: >= 3.3.0 and <= 4.2.0

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper version 4.3.0. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

The RemoteQueryCachePlugin is not enabled by default. Customers who cannot immediately upgrade can mitigate this issue by not enabling the RemoteQueryCachePlugin, or by restricting write access to the shared cache so that only trusted principals can write to it.

References:

CVE-2026-18061
GHSA-fpvp-qwgm-v6h9

CVE-2026-89065 and CVE-2026-89066: Issue with projen - Path traversal and OS command injection

Bulletin ID: 2026-108-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 09/11/2026 09:00 AM PDT

Description:

projen is an open-source tool for defining and synthesizing software project configurations as code. AWS identified two issues in projen affecting the generated file manifest cleanup component and the task synthesis component.

CVE-2026-89065 — Relative path traversal in the generated file manifest cleanup component in projen before 0.101.37 might allow context-dependent attackers to recursively delete files and directories outside the project directory, via crafted entries in the version-controlled generated file manifest (.projen/files.json) that is consumed during project synthesis. The corrected containment check is automatically applied by the projen runtime the next time it is run.
CVE-2026-89066 — Improper neutralization of special elements used in an OS command in the task synthesis component in projen before 0.103.0 might allow context-dependent attackers to execute arbitrary commands on a developer workstation or continuous integration runner via shell metacharacters in project configuration values and repository file names that are interpolated into generated task definitions in .projen/tasks.json.

Impacted versions:

All projen versions before 0.101.37 (CVE-2026-89065)
All projen versions before 0.103.0 (CVE-2026-89066)

Resolution:

CVE-2026-89065 has been addressed in projen version 0.101.37. Upgrading to 0.101.37 or later is sufficient; re-synthesis is not required.
CVE-2026-89066 has been addressed in projen version 0.103.0. After upgrading, you must re-synthesize your project to regenerate .projen/tasks.json with the corrected task definitions. Upgrading alone is not sufficient because the generated task definition file is committed to the repository.

We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

CVE-2026-89065: Review the version control history of .projen/files.json for entries that escape the project directory and remove them prior to running projen.
CVE-2026-89066: Audit project configuration values — including LambdaFunctionOptions.entrypoint, AddBundleOptions fields, JestOptions.extraCliOptions, PytestOptions.testMatch, ReleaseOptions.artifactsDirectory, and other properties listed in the advisory — for shell metacharacters and remove or escape them prior to running projen.

References:

CVE-2026-89065
GHSA-7p65-6x86-v7f3
CVE-2026-89066
GHSA-q6g4-h6vc-vqm8

CVE-2026-89049 - Server-side request forgery in the Session Manager port forwarding functionality in AWS Systems Manager Agent

Bulletin ID: 2026-107-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 09/10/2026 11:30 AM PDT

Description:

AWS Systems Manager Agent (SSM Agent) is software that runs on managed nodes (EC2 instances, on-premises servers, and other supported machines) and processes requests from the AWS Systems Manager service, enabling capabilities including Session Manager port forwarding to remote hosts. We identified CVE-2026-89049, a server-side request forgery issue in the remote-host port forwarding functionality. Due to improper validation of equivalent address representations, an authenticated user with port-forwarding permission could bypass the remote destination denylist and reach link-local endpoints, potentially obtaining the managed instance's temporary IAM role credentials and acting with that role's permissions from outside the instance.

Impacted versions: < 3.3.4851.0 (all versions supporting remote-host port forwarding)

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in SSM Agent version 3.3.4851.0. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

Until the agent is upgraded, restrict use of the AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost document by scoping ssm:StartSession IAM permissions and SSM document permissions so that untrusted principals cannot start remote-host port-forwarding sessions.

CVE-2026-111943: eMudhra intermediate CA key recovery in AWS trust bundles

Bulletin ID: 2026-150-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 10/24/2026 20:00 PM PDT

Summary:

AWS-owned TLS trust bundles are certificate stores used by AWS services to validate outbound TLS connections to customer-configured endpoints, including identity provider endpoints, origin servers, and webhook destinations. We identified CVE-2026-111943, a cryptographic key-generation issue affecting an external Certificate Authority (eMudhra/emSign), whose intermediate CA private keys were trivially recoverable due to catastrophic entropy failures in P-384 key generation. Eight intermediate CA private keys (six TLS, two code-signing) were generated with scalar values of small integers, making them mathematically recoverable without specialized tooling. Please note, customers whose TLS clients enforce certificate revocation checking (OCSP or CRL fail-closed) are not affected, as the issuing CA revoked the affected intermediates on 2026-10-18, and the cross-signing CA revoked its copies on 2026-10-19.

Affected roots:

AAA Certificate Services (SPKI SHA-256: bd153ed7b0434f6886b17bce8bbe84ed340c7132d702a8f4fa318f756ecbd6f3)
emSign Root TLS CA – G3 (SPKI SHA-256: c619e4780ed8e0abeda24ad732567de4383a7ea941338f6d1a7d1b49ac792fe9)
emSign ECC Root CA – G3 (SPKI SHA-256: 8d417db2dd8bf5e3084d1e3f196d583849d81bdd4c00c70b9d39369e96b8c782)

Current Mitigation Status:

Root removal changes for the shared AWS trust store were merged and deployed to the live version set on 2026-10-21.
AWS SDK for Python (boto3 / botocore) was updated and released to PyPI as version 1.43.117.
Amazon CloudFront is deploying root removal from the edge CA bundle by the target date of 2026-10-28.
Amazon Linux 2 and Amazon Linux 2023 updates are available now. Customers should update the ca-certificates package: sudo yum update ca-certificates. Please follow ALAS CVE-2026-113470 and CVE-2026-111943 for more details.
Amazon Corretto has released updated JDK versions across all supported lines with the affected roots removed.
Bottlerocket is publishing updated AMIs targeted for 2026-10-26, with the latest AMI parameters updated in commercial regions by 2026-10-28.
Application Load Balancer is removing the affected roots from the trust store used to validate identity provider endpoints for OIDC and JWT authentication. Application Load Balancers with OIDC or JWT authentication enabled are being updated between 2026-10-29 and 2026-10-31, and newly created Application Load Balancers are protected by 2026-11-02. Customers using OIDC or JWT authentication on Application Load Balancers are being notified through AWS Health. If an identity provider certificate chains to one of the affected roots, replace it with a certificate from an AWS-trusted Certificate Authority by 2026-10-28.
AWS Security Token Service (STS) and Amazon Cognito have completed deploying trust store updates, removing the affected roots used to validate outbound TLS connections to identity provider endpoints.

CVE-2026-85228 - Integer overflow in tensor buffer validation in Deep Java Library

Bulletin ID: 2026-106-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 09/10/2026 10:30 AM PDT

Description:

Deep Java Library (DJL) is an open-source, engine-agnostic Java framework for deep learning, developed and maintained by Amazon. AWS identified CVE-2026-85228, an integer overflow in the tensor buffer validation component of DJL on all platforms. A crafted tensor payload declaring a shape whose computed byte size exceeds the 32-bit signed integer range causes the size to wrap, allowing an undersized buffer to pass validation; a subsequent tensor operation then reads out of bounds. If leveraged, a remote, unauthenticated actor could obtain information from adjacent process memory or cause a denial of service. A fix for this issue has been released and we recommend users of DJL upgrade to version 0.37.0 or later.

Impacted versions: >=0.13.0 AND <=0.36.0

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in ai.djl:api version 0.37.0. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

There is no workaround other than upgrading. Until you can upgrade, only accept tensor input from trusted sources and avoid exposing raw-tensor ("binary mode") inference endpoints backed by native Java engines to untrusted callers.

References:

CVE-2026-87912 and CVE-2026-87913: Missing S3 bucket ownership verification in the AWS Security Agent plugin for aws-agents-for-devsecops and MCP Server

Bulletin ID: 2026-105-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 09/10/2026 08:30 AM PDT

Description:

AWS Security Agent is a managed AWS service that provides AI-powered code security reviews, threat modeling, and penetration testing.

We identified CVE-2026-87912, where a missing S3 bucket ownership verification in the AWS Security Agent plugin in Amazon aws-agents-for-devsecops before version 1.1.0 might allow remote attackers to obtain the private source archive of a scanned workspace, including credentials and infrastructure state contained in that archive, via a pre-registered storage bucket whose name is derived from a publicly known account identifier.

We identified CVE-2026-87913, where a missing S3 bucket ownership verification in the AWS Security Agent MCP server before 0.2.0 might allow remote attackers to obtain the private source archive of a scanned workspace, including credentials and infrastructure state contained in that archive, via a pre-registered storage bucket whose name is derived from a publicly known account identifier.

Impacted versions:

<=1.0.0
>=0.1.0 AND <=0.1.5

Resolution:

This issues has been addressed in agent-toolkit-for-aws and awslabs.security-agent-mcp-server version 0.2.0. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

Upgrading does not release a bucket name that a third party has already registered. We recommend that you verify the scan-input bucket security-agent-scans-<account-id>-<region> in your account is owned by your own account. As a precaution, you can pre-create that bucket in your own account before first use so that the predictable name cannot be registered by another account.

CVE-2026-87911 - Read-only enforcement bypass enabling operating system command execution in the SQL validation component of Amazon awslabs postgres-mcp-server

Bulletin ID: 2026-104-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 09/09/2026 12:30 PM PDT

Description:

awslabs.postgres-mcp-server is a python package that implements a Postgres MCP server. We found CVE-2026-87911, where an OS command injection weakness in the read-only enforcement of the SQL validation component in Amazon awslabs postgres-mcp-server before 1.1.7 might allow an unauthenticated actor to execute operating system commands on the host of a self-managed PostgreSQL server by placing a crafted COPY ... TO PROGRAM statement into content that is processed when an authenticated user interacts with the MCP server in its default read-only mode.

Impacted versions:

awslabs.postgres-mcp-server before 1.1.7, self-managed PostgreSQL deployment profile (PG_WIRE_PROTOCOL connection method) where the configured database role holds superuser or pg_execute_server_program.

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in awslabs postgres-mcp-server (python package) version 1.1.7 in pypi.

Workarounds:

The strongest control is to connect the MCP server using a dedicated Postgres role that has only the privileges it actually needs, so that the database itself enforces the boundary regardless of what SQL reaches it. In particular:

Do not connect as a superuser, rds_superuser, or the cluster master user. Those roles bypass row-level security, can read credential catalogs (pg_authid, pg_user_mappings), and can terminate other sessions.
For read-only use, grant only CONNECT + USAGE + SELECT on the schemas the agent needs, and force read-only transactions at the role level.
For read/write use, grant only the specific INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE privileges required, scoped to the necessary schemas and tables.

Combining a minimal-privilege role (database-enforced) with the blocklist (application-enforced) gives you defense in depth: even if a query slips past the blocklist, the role's privileges still bound what it can do.

References:

CVE-2026-87911
GHSA-fph8-pg5w-78fv

Acknowledgement:

We would like to thank Mordehai Attia (Corsen AI) and Ryan von Brubeck for collaborating on this issue through the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

node2shell-lab
A lightweight, single-container pentest lab about an engine-level decompression
bug: the app layer is boring, the decoder underneath it is not.
You are triage on-call for PacketLedger, a freight-manifest gateway for the
harbor district. Routine traffic, routine app — except the intake API happily
decompresses brotli request bodies on a runtime that ships a very interesting
advisory. The attestation desk upstairs refuses to hand over the sealed proof
until someone can demonstrate an engine incident. Three crashes. That's the policy.

📌 Real CVE, invented story — please read.
CVE-2026-111497 is real: an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder
bundled with Node.js (Google Brotli 1.0.3–1.2.0), published to NVD on
2026-10-22 and fixed in Node 24.22.1 by the
October 21, 2026 Node.js security releases
(NVD entry).
"Node2Shell" is this lab's nickname for the bug, not an official name — and
not a promise (see win condition below). docs/ADVISORY.md wraps the real
facts in an in-world storyline: the story is fiction, the CVE is not.

🎯 Honest win condition. This lab is gated on a demonstrated engine
crash (a reliable DoS-class primitive), not on catching a shell. Full RCE
landing is heap-layout dependent and explicitly bonus — see
"Platform notes". If you get a SIGSEGV and the crash counter moves, you have
won the gate; do not burn your evening chasing /bin/sh.

What's inside

2 flags (OffSec-style pair): a local flag reachable through an
application-layer primitive, and a proof flag held behind an engine-level gate.
App surface: ~200 LOC of Node/Express. The real target is what lives below it.
No credentials to find, no rabbit-hole content. Small by design; clone-to-playable
in under two minutes.

Difficulty
Medium-hard (≈3.5 / 5) for anyone who has not worked a decompression bug before;
medium if you have. The steep part is not the payload — it's realizing where
the bug lives and how the engine wants to be fed.
Calibration: the full solve chain has been verified end-to-end by a local LLM agent.
Quick start
Prerequisites: Docker Engine (or Docker Desktop) with the compose plugin, plus
Python 3 (stdlib only, no pip installs — needed to run the reference PoC
generator referenced by hint-ladder step 5).
The image is linux/amd64 — on Apple Silicon Docker Desktop runs it under
Rosetta (supported, see platform notes); on Windows use WSL2 + Docker Desktop.
git clone <repo-url> node2shell-lab && cd node2shell-lab

# Build (flags are build args — defaults work out of the box, set your own to be unique)
docker compose build \
--build-arg LOCAL_FLAG='FLAG{y…l_1}' \
--build-arg PROOF_FLAG='FLAG{y…f_1}'

docker compose up -d

# Confirm it is alive (published on 0.0.0.0:18993 — all interfaces; add a
# 127.0.0.1: prefix to the compose port mapping to tighten it to loopback)
curl http://127.0.0.1:18993/api/health

Entry point: http://127.0.0.1:18993/ — the landing page lists the public intake surface.
Ops:
./reset.sh # factory reset: wipes the crash ledger, re-seals the attestation
./teardown.sh # stop and remove the container, free port 18993
docker compose logs -f gateway # supervisor + worker log stream

The brief

GET / lists endpoints and accepted encodings. Read it, then read /api/health.
The attestation desk (GET /api/attest) states its unseal policy in the 403
body itself — the knowledge gate is knowing what to send, not guessing state.
One advisory document ships in this repo (docs/ADVISORY.md). Consider it the
only intel you get. Read it twice.
Flags never appear in any world-readable path. If you find a file you "shouldn't"
be able to read, you're playing right.

Work top-down; peel one rung at a time.

Recon is the whole first act. Enumerate what GET / advertises. The health

supervisor counting crashes implies about this deployment's history.

// DECRYPTED: 2026-10-24 | AUTHOR: msdbg
CVE-2026-109618: PHP Zend Engine Non-Local Jump (longjmp) Use-After-Free in RFC 1867 Upload Progress Lifecycle
INTRO and notes
this is not a news post, it is a technical writeup about the Viral PHP Bug, you might already have scratched the surface about this RCE, so let's directly dive in to the UAF itself.
Please note the php version here is 8.3.12.
The Root Cause analysis
this memory safety flaw in PHP's Zend Engine comes from mismatch between C's non-local jump exception handling _zend_bailout() via longjmp() and internal pointer caching within extension ext/session/session.c
When processing multipart form data payloads according to RFC 1867, When session upload progress is enabled session.upload_progress.enabled = 1 PHP's upload progress tracking caches internal heap addresses zval *post_bytes_processed directly addressing dynamically managed array memory Bucket *arData).
If an allocation failure occurs due to ZendMM quota exhaustion memory_limit, the engine issues an longjmp() exception.
Triggered during MULTIPART_EVENT_FILE_START
progress->post_bytes_processed = zend_hash_str_find(Z_ARRVAL(progress->data), "bytes_processed", sizeof("bytes_processed") - 1);
This exit abandons C call frames and bypasses clean termination logic MULTIPART_EVENT_END
During subsequent request shutdown (php_request_shutdown()), the session hash table is destroyed and its arData memory slab is returned to ZendMM's small bin LIFO free list. But, the global progress structure (PS(rfc1867_progress)) remains allocated and retains the dangling heap pointer. In persistent SAPIs (PHP-FPM and PHP CLI Server), subsequent memory allocations reuse this exact address,
converting an unhandled memory exception into deterministic Type Confusion and Remote Code Execution (RCE), Under normal execution, this pointer is safely destroyed at the end of the request via php_session_rfc1867_cleanup() or during MULTIPART_EVENT_END
In PHP Zend Engine 3+, a HashTable does not store elements as isolated heap nodes. Instead, buckets are packed into an allocated array pointed to by ht->arData (Bucket *arData). Any operation that inserts keys, rehashes, (IS_UNDEF) reallocates the entire arData buffer via erealloc() or pemalloc(). C pointer pointing to a bucket or zval inside arData (&arData[idx].val) is invalidated the moment the array shifts.
the Zend Engine handles fatal errors like hitting the memory_limit using _zend_bailout(), which the C longjmp() function. When longjmp() executes it unwinds the stack back to php_request_shutdown(), bypassing the standard sequential destructors in session.c. The progress->post_bytes_processed pointer is never nulled out.
When an out-of-memory error occurs, ZendMM calls zend_error_noreturn(E_ERROR, ...), which enters _zend_bailout()
ZEND_API ZEND_COLD ZEND_NORETURN void _zend_bailout(char *filename, uint32_t lineno) {
longjmp(EG(bailout), FAILURE);
}

longjmp() restores the stack previously saved by setjmp() in php_execute_script(). It unwinds the C stack, discarding local stack frames and bypassing any cleanup instructions.
PS(rfc1867_progress) was created under the assumption that execution always proceeds sequentially from MULTIPART_EVENT_START to MULTIPART_EVENT_END. While $_SESSION is destroyed in php_rshutdown_session_globals(), PS(rfc1867_progress) is only freed and nulled in MULTIPART_EVENT_END.
An OOM bailout prevents execution from ever reaching MULTIPART_EVENT_END, leaving PS(rfc1867_progress)->post_bytes_processed dangling in global memory pointing to an address that ZendMM has already marked as free.

PoC and UAF Exploitation.
the exploit relies on precise heap grooming to force the bailout at the exact moment the pointer is live.

title: Remote Access Trojan.  Fancy name, simple idea: something that looks harmless but lets an attacker control your device.  Here’s how it works, minus the jargon. https://www.1bluebass.com/2026/08/18/rat/?utm_source=mastodon&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=fedica-tmack-security-pipeline #InfoSec #ITAcronyms #RAT
text:
A Remote Access Trojan is a type of malicious software that allows cyber attackers to gain unauthorized access and control over a victim’s computer or network.  RATs are designed to operate stealthily, enabling attackers to perform various malicious activities without the victim’s knowledge.
Key Features of RATs

Remote Control: RATs enable attackers to remotely control a victim’s device as if they were sitting in front of it. This control can include accessing files, running applications, and even using the webcam or microphone.
Stealth Operations: Many RATs are designed to be stealthy, meaning they can operate in the background without alerting the user.  They often disguise themselves as legitimate software or hide their presence within the system.
Data Exfiltration: Attackers can use RATs to steal sensitive information from the victim’s device, such as passwords, financial data, and personal files.  This stolen data can be used for identity theft, financial fraud, or sold on the dark web.
Keylogging: Some RATs include keylogging capabilities, which record every keystroke made by the user.  This feature allows attackers to capture passwords, credit card numbers, and other sensitive information.
File Management: RATs often provide attackers with the ability to upload and download files from the victim’s device.  This can be used to install additional malware or exfiltrate sensitive data.
Persistence: Many RATs are designed to maintain persistence on the infected device, meaning they can survive reboots and attempts to remove them.  They may install themselves as a service or modify system settings to ensure they remain active.

How Cyber Attackers Use RATs

Initial Infection: Cyber attackers typically use various methods to deliver RATs to victims.  Common techniques include phishing emails, malicious downloads, or exploiting vulnerabilities in software.  Once the victim unknowingly executes the RAT, it installs itself on their device.
Establishing Control: After installation, the RAT connects to a command-and-control (C2) server controlled by the attacker.  This connection allows the attacker to send commands to the infected device and receive data from it.
Executing Malicious Activities: Once control is established, attackers can perform a range of malicious activities, including:

Stealing Information: Accessing sensitive files, capturing login credentials, and exfiltrating data.
Spying: Using the victim’s webcam or microphone to monitor their activities.
Installing Additional Malware: Deploying other types of malware, such as ransomware or spyware, to further compromise the victim’s system.

Covering Tracks: To avoid detection, attackers may use techniques to hide the RAT’s presence, such as deleting logs or using encryption to obfuscate communications with the C2 server.

Prevention and Protection

Use Antivirus Software: Regularly update and run antivirus software to detect and remove RATs and other malware.
Be Cautious with Emails: Avoid opening attachments or clicking on links in unsolicited emails, as these are common methods for delivering RATs.
Keep Software Updated: Regularly update operating systems and applications to patch vulnerabilities that attackers may exploit.
Enable Firewalls: Use firewalls to monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic, which can help block unauthorized access.
Educate Users: Training users to recognize phishing attempts and suspicious activities can significantly reduce the risk of RAT infections.

A Remote Access Trojan is a powerful and dangerous type of malware that allows cyber attackers to gain unauthorized control over a victim’s device.  By understanding how RATs operate and the methods attackers use to deploy them, individuals and organizations can take proactive steps to protect themselves from these threats.

title: Panasonic: a member of an HR system project uploaded data on about 334,000 current and former employees and family members to an external generative AI service the company had banned. Training was off, the provider kept deleted data for 30 days.In our view, a written ban isn't a control, and even approved AI leaves hard calls to staff, especially for client data that isn't personal data. Time to rethink DLP across every channel.https://japancyberwatch.com/articles/panasonic-generative-ai-employee-data-upload-2026#infosec #privacy #japan
text:
Key takeaways

Panasonic Operational Excellence, which runs shared back-office functions for Japan's Panasonic Group, said on October 23, 2026 that a member of an HR system project had uploaded personal data to an external generative AI service the company had banned.
About 334,000 people are affected: roughly 75,000 current employees and 178,000 former employees going back to 1978, with employee numbers, addresses, phone numbers and emails, and 81,000 family members registered as emergency contacts, with names as well.
It was not an attack. Panasonic says the AI provider told it the training setting was off and the data was not used to answer anyone else, but that deleted data is kept for 30 days; that period ended on October 25.
Panasonic reported the incident to the privacy regulator on September 29 and published its notice almost four weeks later, as a substitute for notifying each person. It has not named the AI service.
In our view, it is a clear case of shadow AI: a written ban that nothing technical enforced, in a project that had a large extract of personal data to hand. Blocking every unapproved AI service is hard to run; detecting personal data and blocking bulk uploads is the more realistic control. Even with approved AI, deciding what client information may go in is too hard to leave to each employee. It is time to look at technical controls, starting with a fresh look at DLP, since AI services are only one of many places data can go.

What happened#
Panasonic Operational Excellence (PEX) is running a project with its subsidiary Panasonic Digital to introduce a new HR information system for Panasonic Group companies in Japan. During that project, a project member uploaded data from the existing HR system, as it stood in April 2026, to an external generative AI service. PEX prohibits the use of that service.
Panasonic calls it a rule violation by the project member, not an outside attack. After it was discovered, the member deleted the chat history and the data on their work PC. Panasonic has not said when the upload happened, how it was found, why the data was uploaded, or which AI service was used.

What the AI provider said#
Panasonic asked the operator of the AI service what had happened to the data. According to Panasonic, the provider said:

The setting that lets the provider use input data to train its AI was turned off when the data was uploaded, so the data would not appear in answers to other users.
When a user deletes data, the provider still keeps it for 30 days for security and legal compliance, under strict access control, and accesses it only for audits and similar requests.
The data deleted right after discovery would therefore be gone from the provider's systems from October 25.

On that basis, Panasonic says the data will not be used further, and that it has found no sign of publication or misuse. It tells the people affected that they do not need to do anything.

text:
You're using a suspiciously old browser
You're probably reading this page because you've attempted to access
some part of my blog (Wandering Thoughts) or
CSpace, the wiki thing it's part of. Unfortunately
you're using a browser version that my anti-crawler precautions consider
suspicious, most often because it's too old (most often this applies to
versions of Chrome). Unfortunately, as of early 2025 there's a plague
of high volume crawlers (apparently in part to gather data for LLM
training) that use a variety of old browser user agents, especially
Chrome user agents. To reduce the load on
Wandering Thoughts I'm experimenting with
(attempting to) block all of them, and you've run into this.

If this is in error and you're using a current version of your
browser of choice, you can contact me at my current place at the
university (you should be able to work out the email address
from that). If possible, please let me know what browser you're
using and so on, ideally with its exact User-Agent string.

A special note to people using Inoreader (the feed reader)

I am not blocking Inoreader's feed fetcher or considering it to be
too old, and it routinely fetches feeds from me. I don't know why
Inoreader is showing you this page. It is possible that they're
periodically trying to fetch feeds or pages with an old browser
HTTP User-Agent (or an actual old browser) and taking the results
of that fetch (this page) as what they should show people instead
of the results of their syndication feed fetcher agents. This is a
bad mistake today; the results
of modern HTTP fetches depend partly on the HTTP User-Agent used.

A special note to people using Feedly (the feed reader)

Much like Inoreader, Feedly is periodically fetching my syndication
feeds with a fake, old browser HTTP User-Agent header, which fails,
and is then grimly latching on to the results for their actual feed
fetching with their regular Feedly HTTP User-Agent. There is nothing
I can do about this; you should contact Feedly support, if you can
find them. See this
comment of mine in Wandering Thoughts for more details.

A special note for people using Vivaldi

Due to an ongoing attack, you may need to change
the
"User Agent Brand Masking" setting so that your Vivaldi identifies
itself as Vivaldi, instead of Google Chrome. This applies to even
the current version of Vivaldi.

A special note for people using archive.*

You may be seeing this through archive.today, archive.ph, archive.is,
and so on. Unfortunately, archive.* crawls pages to archive in a way that
is impossible to distinguish from malicious actors. They use old Chrome
User-Agent values, crawl from IP address blocks that are widely distributed
and not clearly identified as theirs, and some of their IP addresses have
falsified reverse DNS entries that claim they are googlebot IP addresses
(which is something that is normally done only by quite bad actors). I
suggest that you use archive.org, which is a better behaved archival
crawler and can crawl my blog (Wandering Thoughts).

Chris Siebenmann, 2025-02-17

Unpatched Tailscale SSH Flaws Could Let a Hacked Device Reach Root on Other ServersSwati KhandelwalOct 25, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security

//<![CDATA[

//]]>

A single hacked device on a Tailscale network can be used to gain root access to other servers it can reach, according to a security researcher who published the findings this week.

The attack requires two things: Tailscale SSH set up to allow port forwarding, and an attacker who already controls one device that the network's access rules permit to connect to the target.

The findings were published on October 25 in a report called Tailworm by Erica Windisch of Cyberdione Labs. Windisch tested Tailscale version 1.104.2 and headscale version 0.29.5, the self-hosted server some networks use to run Tailscale instead of the company's hosted service, over three days in a lab.

The report describes tests on that software, not attacks against real networks. As of publication, Tailscale had issued no security bulletin, no CVE identifier, and no fixed version.

Tailscale has responded in public. Mike Shaver, the company's vice president of engineering, wrote on Reddit that Tailscale had received the report, had already been looking at the same areas with outside security specialists, and had found issues it is working to fix. Shaver said the company is still working out which setups are affected, and that it is "not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH."

Tailscale SSH does not work like a normal SSH server. Rather than checking a connecting user's password or key, it identifies the device, and a single access rule decides whether that device may open an SSH session to a target.

Because of this, the attack needs no stolen passwords or keys. It needs a foothold on one device first, which the report says an attacker can get the usual ways: a vulnerable web application, a poisoned software package, phishing, or stolen login details. Tailscale does not create that first foothold.

How much an administrator can do about it depends on where the network is run. On Tailscale's hosted service, forwarding can be switched off per rule. On headscale version 0.29.5, forwarding cannot be turned off at all. The report says every SSH grant there should therefore be treated as giving root on the target.

In the lab, Windisch showed the problem in stages. Using standard SSH port forwarding, an ordinary session caused the root-level Tailscale process to connect to a system socket that only root should access, and the test gained root and read the system password file almost immediately, without administrator rights.

A second method replaced a root-owned socket with the attacker's, allowing direct root command execution against certain services.

A third method defeated a safety check meant to limit which files forwarding can access by racing the system between when it checks a file path and when it uses it. That chain went further in the lab, the report says: it captured a key used to enroll new devices and used the key to join an attacker's own machine to the network as a trusted server.

That last step worked from start to finish only on networks where Tailscale's Tailnet Lock feature was not enabled. On networks that do, the needed secrets were captured in transit, but the final step was not completed.

Windisch describes the overall result as "wormable." In the lab, one compromised device could spread to every device that the access rules allow, with no passwords, no stolen keys, and no user action, in under a second per step.

In the report's words, "the mesh converts one ordinary foothold into fleet-wide privileged access at machine speed." That spread was measured in a lab, not seen on real networks.

The report names two things that held it back: access rules written as single […]

text: 2026-10-26 · Daily security tipsIs your site missing basic security headers?Security headers are small instructions your server sends with every page. Many AI-built and quickly deployed apps ship with none of them.Check: open your live site, go to DevTools > Network, click the first request and read the Response Headers. Look for Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options (or a CSP frame-ancestors rule), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy.Fix: add them in your host's config (vercel.json, netlify.toml, _headers) or your framework's headers setting. Start with nosniff, a referrer policy and frame protection, which rarely break anything. Roll out Content-Security-Policy carefully, in report-only mode first.Headers are not a substitute for fixing leaked keys or open database tables, but they are cheap protection.

PingCAP Data Breach Exposes Source Code and Cloud Control Plane Records

PingCAP, the developer of the TiDB distributed database, confirmed a data breach involving the theft of source code and customer records. The incident occurred between September 9 and October 7, 2026. The cyber extortion group FulcrumSec claims responsibility for the breach and alleges it stole 10.6 TB of data. This includes TiDB Cloud control-plane records and hundreds of private source-code repositories.The attackers used stolen service account credentials to enter PingCAP's internal environment. # Three Billion Records Leaked. Your Past is Now Public.

The most surprising number on the wire this afternoon isn't a CVSS score or a ransom demand. It’s 3 billion.

A background check company has confirmed a breach of nearly 3 billion records. For those struggling with the scale, that isn't just a "large" leak; it's an extinction-level event for anonymity. When a social media site leaks, you lose your handle and maybe some embarrassing DMs. When a background check firm goes under, the attackers don't just get emails; they get the curated, verified history of human existence—criminal records, employment gaps, addresses, and the kind of deep-tissue personal data that is meant to be gated by "trust."

The incentive here is simple: these companies sell certainty. They charge employers a premium to guarantee that a candidate is who they say they are. But the internal incentive for the vendor is usually to maximize the volume of checks while minimizing the cost of the vault. If you're processing billions of records, security becomes a cost center that eats into the margin of every $50 check performed.

The second-order effect here is where it gets ugly. This isn't just about identity theft; it's about the weaponization of history. Every HR department that used this vendor now holds "verified" data that has been touched by criminals. More importantly, imagine the leverage an attacker has when they can cross-reference a person's current employer with their most private failures from a decade ago. We’ve moved past simple credential stuffing into the realm of institutionalized blackmail.

Why do we continue to outsource our most sensitive verification processes to entities that treat three billion lives like an unsecured spreadsheet?

Then there is Loblaw. The Canadian grocery giant finally admitted that a data breach from March affected roughly 2 million people.

Note the timeline. It is now October 25. There is a seven-month gap between the event and the announcement. In the world of corporate communications, that gap is where "we are investigating" transforms into "we've decided how to frame this." Loblaw is now offering free credit monitoring—the standard, hollow peace offering of the modern breach.

This rhymes perfectly with the Yahoo leaks of a decade ago, where the delay was measured in years. The parallel breaks, however, in the nature of the data. We aren't talking about passwords anymore; we're talking about the intersection of food supply and personal identity. When you buy groceries, you aren't signing a waiver to have your data sit in a lukewarm bucket for seven months before being told it’s gone.

The shift from explanation to excuse happens the moment they mention "credit monitoring." It is an admission that the damage is already done and the only thing they can provide is a digital bandage for a severed limb. The incentive for the delay was likely a desire to clear the quarterly books or avoid a PR nightmare during a specific retail cycle. They gambled that the silence would be cheaper than the fallout.

While we're talking about the "elite" getting hit, PwC confirmed that the Everest ransomware group walked away with 590 GB of company data. There is something deliciously ironic about one of the world's most expensive consulting firms—people who literally get paid to tell other companies how to manage risk—being unable to stop a ransomware group from hauling off half a terabyte of internal files. I suspect the Everest group found the "risk management" folders particularly illuminating.

But if you want to see where policy genuinely fails the person, look at the State Bank of India (SBI).

# The math of the PHP vulnerabilities

70 percent.

That's the number of websites currently at risk thanks to two flaws in PHP. If you're wondering if this affects you, assume it does. When vulnerabilities hit the plumbing of the web, the damage isn't a small circle. It's the whole map.

I've seen this happen before. NotPetya showed us how a single compromised update mechanism could cause a global blackout in hours because everyone trusted the same pipe. This PHP mess is the same brand of fragility. You aren't just worried about your own code here. You're worried about every legacy script and library you've inherited over ten years.

Some analysts are claiming these exploits aren't viable in real production environments. They love calling an exploit sophisticated to explain why it might be hard to execute. I hate that word. Usually, it just means they don't know how the attackers are doing it.

The truth is that viability doesn't matter when 70 percent of the web is a target. An attacker doesn't need a surgical strike if they can throw a net over the ocean. Even if an exploit only works on 1 percent of those sites, that's still millions of holes. I remember cleaning up after Code Red in 2001. The viability argument didn't stop those servers from crashing.

Check the volume this week. We've seen 484 stories on data breaches. Today alone, 15 new vulnerability reports hit the wire. There is a lot of noise, but these PHP flaws are the only thing that should keep you awake. The second-order effects are the problem.

When a foundation like PHP breaks, it isn't just the website owner who suffers. Hosting providers have to deal with massive botnet traffic spikes as attackers scan for holes. Downstream customers have data sitting on servers that haven't been updated since 2019. Insurers will likely find out their cyber coverage doesn't cover a systemic failure of the web's basic building blocks.

Compare this to today's report about the background check company breach where nearly 3 billion records were stolen. That is a tragedy of scale, sure, but it's contained. The data is gone and we manage the fallout. A PHP flaw affecting 70 percent of websites isn't a theft. It's an open door.

Do modern containers and WAFs fix this? No. They just move the bottleneck. If the engine is broken, you've just put a fancy fence around a house with no walls.

What does this actually cost you on a Tuesday? Imagine your site goes dark or becomes a relay for a Mirai-style botnet at 10:00 AM. How long would it take to restore from a backup that isn't also compromised? Most of you haven't even tested those backups in six months.

Windows Server 2016 Support Ends Soon, Plus 2 Stories

Mike York

Daily Briefs
Abandonware, data breach, End of Support, microsoft, Popcorn Time, Quest Diagnostics, Windows Server

Windows Server 2016 has a deadline now, and this one deserves more than a calendar reminder. Microsoft will end extended support on January 12, 2027. The software won’t switch itself off that night, but regular security updates will. For a business that still depends on a 2016 server, “it still works” is about to become the wrong test.

Windows Server 2016 support ends January 12

Microsoft says Windows Server 2016 reaches the end of extended support on January 12, 2027. Datacenter, Standard, Essentials, and MultiPoint Premium are affected. After that date, organizations won’t receive ordinary monthly security updates through the standard lifecycle.

That doesn’t mean the machine stops booting. It means newly discovered flaws can remain open while the server keeps doing whatever the business built around it. And “whatever” can be a lot: Active Directory logins, DNS, shared files, Remote Desktop, an accounting database, a manufacturing application, or the one line-of-business program nobody has touched because the vendor vanished six years ago.

This is why an operating-system upgrade is rarely the whole job. You have to identify the workload, the people and devices that depend on it, the application versions it can support, and the recovery plan if the migration fails. A current backup helps, but only if someone has tested restoring it somewhere other than the server being replaced. The uncomfortable question is simple: if this box disappeared tomorrow, what stops with it?

Microsoft is offering Extended Security Updates through Azure Arc for organizations that need more time. That is a useful bridge, not a modernization strategy. It can keep critical security fixes coming while a migration is finished, but it doesn’t make aging hardware younger, modernize an old application, or remove the operational cost of depending on a platform already past its standard life.

If you own the business rather than the server, ask for a short inventory now: which systems still run 2016, what each one does, who owns the application, whether backups have been restored in a test, and what date the migration will finish. Also ask which version is actually running. A “Windows server” in a closet is not an inventory. We recently saw how routine Windows updates can expose dependencies in on-premises Exchange; a major version migration will find even more of them.

Business IT goes well beyond the website

Your business also depends on workstations, cloud accounts, browsers, Wi-Fi, remote access, collaboration tools, and all the other technology that quietly becomes infrastructure. Raymond Tec works across that whole stack, whether the problem lives on a server, on a desk, or somewhere in between.

Those are still open questions. “The labs kept running” and “patient information stayed private” are two different claims, and Quest has only made the first one.

Email addresses, login metadata, and last-used IP addresses were accessed
Capcom says unauthorized access to CAPCOM ID affected 11,774,247 records worldwide, creating an immediate risk of convincing phishing messages aimed at players.
Capcom confirmed the incident on October 22, 2026, after detecting suspicious activity three days earlier. The affected service is CAPCOM ID, the unified account used for several company web services and required for online play in certain Capcom games.
This is a confirmed compromise of the CAPCOM ID service. It is different from an individual account takeover such as the cases covered in our Roblox account recovery guide. Capcom says its games remain available and the incident does not prevent players from accessing or playing them.

What information was affected
According to Capcom’s official notice, the 11,774,247 affected records include email addresses and system information: the date and time an account was created, the date and time of its last login, the number of logins, and the client IP address used for the last login.
Within that total, 43 records also included a date of birth, gender, country or region, and nickname. Capcom also confirmed that login passwords were changed without authorization on 196 accounts. Those passwords have been reset.
Capcom has not confirmed that passwords originally chosen by customers were exposed. Credit card information was not included among the affected data.
Capcom’s official notice lists 11,774,247 affected records worldwide and 196 accounts with unauthorized password changes. Image credit: Capcom.
Why players should watch their inboxes
The immediate player risk is impersonation. Capcom warns that the exposed information could be misused for fraudulent emails or other messages pretending to come from the company or a related party.
Do not open attachments or follow links in a suspicious message. If an email claims there is a problem with your account, open the official CAPCOM ID website yourself or use Capcom support. This is especially important because convincing branded messages are already a recurring tactic in gaming account and phishing scams.
Capcom says the attack method has been addressed
Capcom detected the activity on October 19 and began blocking access while investigating. The company established an internal incident response headquarters on October 20, then reported the matter to the Osaka Prefectural Police and Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission on October 21.
The company says it has identified and addressed the method used in the attack and completed its emergency response measures. It is contacting affected customers, operating dedicated support channels, and continuing to investigate the full scope of the incident. # Who Actually Owns Your Background Check?

The tech world is a complete disaster right now, and it's the hardest hit sector this week, with 343 stories hitting the wire, and the bleeding hasn't stopped tonight. Look at three specific cases and you can see exactly where we stand; a background check firm lost nearly 3 billion records. Capcom confirmed that over 11.7 million user accounts were breached. Then you have PwC, where the Everest group managed to walk away with 590 GB of data.

Why does the press always obsess over the volume? They talk about billions of rows and gigabytes of theft; they'll call these "sophisticated attacks" or claim that criminals used "military-grade" tools to break encryption. I can't stand that phrase. There isn't such a thing as military-grade encryption, and it's just math that works or math that doesn't. AES-256 isn't the problem here. The math is fine.

What's actually happening here is almost always a key-management failure disguised as a cryptographic breach.

Most companies say they encrypt data at rest. It looks great on a compliance audit. But what happens if an attacker gets into the application server? If that server has permanent, unrestricted permission to ask the database for decrypted plaintext, then the encryption didn't really do much. It was a speed bump. Did the criminals actually break the lock? No. They just found the key taped to the underside of the mat.

To fix this, we need to talk about Envelope Encryption. It’s a simple protocol that prevents a single compromised credential from turning into a catastrophic leak.

Most setups rely on one master key to lock everything down. That's a mistake because if that single key leaks, you're finished. An envelope system is different. You create a unique Data Encryption Key for every piece of data or every user record and use that DEK to encrypt the actual information. Then comes the clever part. You encrypt the DEK using a separate Key Encryption Key, which stays tucked away in a secure vault or a hardware security module.

The encrypted DEK is stored right alongside the encrypted data. To get the plaintext, an attacker needs both the database and the KEK.

AugustAUGUST Kerckhoffs argued over a century ago that a system should be secure even if everything about it is public knowledge except for the key. The problem today isn't that the systems are secret; it's that we treat keys like static passwords instead of ephemeral tokens. When you see nearly 3 billion records walk out the door, you aren't looking at a failure of AES. You're looking at a system where the KEK was effectively public to anyone who breached the app layer.

Some architects will argue that envelope encryption adds too much latency for high-volume systems. They claim the overhead of calling a vault for every record is a performance killer.

That argument is ten years old. Modern caching and regional key management services have pushed that latency down to almost nothing. More importantly, when you're dealing with billions of records, an extra few milliseconds per request is a rounding error (hardly worth mentioning) compared to the cost of losing 3 billion identities in one afternoon.

The second-order effect is where things get ugly. Take the background check company. They aren't the end consumer; they're just a middleman. Now, every corporation that used them to vet employees has a liability on their books. Those companies didn't just outsource a chore; they handed over the PII of their entire staff to a third party with porous key management. The fallout will shift from the breached vendor to the legal departments of every client on their list.

Google has updated its privacy policy to spell out that using personalized artificial intelligence (AI) features in Search or Gemini could allow the company to serve targeted ads to users based on their activity on other connected Google services.

"You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service," reads a policy update effective October 16, 2026.

"For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads."

Google also notes in its revised policy that "We don't show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos, unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads."

News of the policy update was first reported by Android Authority.

Personal Intelligence, unveiled by Google in Gemini in January 2026, allows users to connect other services like Gmail, Google Photos, and YouTube as a way to provide tailored answers in combination with their chat history preferences.

The feature is currently rolling out as a beta to eligible users over the age of 18 globally, except in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, the U.K., and Nigeria.

It's worth noting that the policy states it doesn't use content from Gmail, Drive, or Photos to personalize ads by default. However, that changes should users opt to share photos or emails with AI Mode and other Search tools via the Personal Intelligence feature.

In other words, if users interact with AI Mode or Gemini while Personal Intelligence is enabled, the data that informs those answers (i.e., content from Gmail or Photos) could be used as a signal to serve targeted ads. The privacy policy aims to make it clear that feeding personal data into its AI tools could contribute to ad personalization.

Users should be mindful of the privacy trade-off when connecting their apps to enable AI features. Those who prefer to opt out can do so by selecting the apps they want to disconnect from Personal Intelligence or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings ("www.google[.]com/search-personalization").

In January 2026, OpenAI began showing ads to logged-in adult U.S. users in both the free and ChatGPT Go tiers, while emphasizing that users' data and conversations are protected and never sold to advertisers. It has also said the ads do not influence responses from the chatbot, and that users are in control of the experience.

Earlier this week, the AI company said it's expanded advertising on ChatGPT to 26 more countries, ​bringing the total to 89. This includes 14 more ​Latin American countries and several markets across Europe, Africa, and Asia.

"We keep conversations private from advertisers and do not sell customer data," OpenAI stressed. "Ads in ChatGPT are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT's answers, and advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides."
